The paper was published in Fatigue of Aircraft Structures Vol. 1 (2009), pages 37-41.
Composite structures have been used in sport aviation (mainly gliders) for approximately forty years before this paper was written.
The inspection of MiG-29 vertical stabilizers covered more than 30 aircraft with a total inspection area exceeding 360 square meters.
Approximately 11 square meters of composite surface area were inspected per MiG-29 aircraft.
The MAUS® system is a hybrid, fully portable inspection system capable of performing multiple NDT techniques.
The MAUS® system can perform inspections on horizontal and vertical inverted surfaces using a flexible track system.
Amplitude C-scan mode is particularly useful for detection of disbonds in composite structures.
TOF (Time Of Flight) C-scan mode provides information about composite skin thickness and delamination depth.
The B1-PW-5 glider wing has a sandwich skin with a 5 mm DIVINYCELL foam core.
Ultrasonic signals experience high attenuation in foam cores, making traditional UT less effective for sandwich structures.
Mechanical Impedance Analysis (MIA) uses low-frequency signals that are more effective for foam core inspection than ultrasonic testing.
Test probes with disbonds as small as 1 square millimeter and 1.5 square millimeters were successfully detected using MIA.
Damages in MiG-29 vertical stabilizers were found to occur randomly across different aircraft, necessitating periodic inspection.
The Air Force Institute of Technology in Warsaw, Poland conducted the research presented in this paper.
Automated inspection procedures increased both reliability and speed while reducing human factor errors in measurement.
The paper discusses three approaches to implementing Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) sensor networks.
In-situ SHM sensors are permanently installed in the structure and require aircraft to be on the ground for diagnostics.
Advanced SHM systems can transmit collected data wirelessly to maintenance personnel in real-time.
Composite airframes are typically more integral than metal airframes, allowing for different design approaches.
The anisotropic nature of composites means their characteristics depend on the direction along which they are considered.
Resonance and Shearography techniques were found effective for detecting core-skin disbonds in sandwich structures.
Laser Shearography is described as very fast and sensitive, especially for thin skin sandwiches, but provides only qualitative results.
The paper emphasizes the necessity for periodic inspection of composite skins due to random damage distribution.
Automated scanning was necessary because manual hand scanning was very difficult or impossible when work had to be performed on the aircraft.
The research included inspection of F-16 horizontal stabilizers and W-3 helicopter main rotor blades in addition to MiG-29 vertical stabilizers.
